visuals.title: Where the problem is
visuals.text: Blood counts fall because the marrow fails or is crowded out; the spleen and nodes may enlarge.

glossary.RBC: Red blood cell: carries oxygen using haemoglobin.
glossary.RBCs: Red blood cells, which carry oxygen using haemoglobin.
glossary.WBC: White blood cell: part of the immune system fighting infection.
glossary.WBCs: White blood cells, which fight infection.
glossary.WCC: White cell count: the total number of white blood cells in the blood.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: a blood test measuring haemoglobin, white cells, platelets and red cell indices.
glossary.Cell lines: The three families of blood cells made by the marrow: red cells, white cells and platelets.
glossary.Platelets: Small cell fragments that plug damaged vessels and start clotting.
glossary.Anaemia: A low haemoglobin level, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.
glossary.Pallor: Unusually pale skin or conjunctivae, often a sign of anaemia.
glossary.Lymphadenopathy: Enlarged lymph nodes, from infection, inflammation or cancer.
glossary.Radiotherapy: Cancer treatment using ionising radiation, which can damage the bone marrow.
glossary.Chemotherapy: Drugs that kill rapidly dividing cells, used for cancer; they also suppress the marrow.
glossary.Bone marrow: Soft tissue inside bones where blood cells are made.
glossary.Bone marrow failure: The marrow cannot make enough blood cells, usually because stem cells are lost.
glossary.Bone marrow infiltration: Abnormal cells, such as cancer, fill the marrow and push out normal blood-forming cells.
glossary.Marrow suppression: Reduced blood cell production by the marrow, often from drugs.
glossary.Leukaemia: A cancer of blood-forming cells in which abnormal white cells fill the marrow and blood.
glossary.Lymphoma: A cancer of lymphocytes, usually arising in lymph nodes.
glossary.Metastasis: Spread of a cancer from its original site to another part of the body.
glossary.ALL: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia: rapid build-up of immature lymphoid blasts, commonest in children.
glossary.Dysplastic: Abnormal in shape and maturation; a sign of disordered cell development.
glossary.Pelger-Huët anomaly: Neutrophils with hyposegmented or bilobed nuclei, a classic film finding in MDS.
glossary.Hyposegmented: A neutrophil nucleus with fewer lobes than normal.
glossary.Bilobed: Having two lobes, as in the neutrophil nucleus in Pelger-Huët anomaly.
glossary.Myeloid: Relating to the marrow cell line that makes red cells, granulocytes, monocytes and platelets.
glossary.Clonal: Arising from a single abnormal cell, so all its descendants carry the same defect.
glossary.Precursors: Immature cells in the marrow that develop into mature blood cells.
glossary.HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus, which can suppress the marrow and cause cytopenias.
glossary.B12: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin), needed for DNA synthesis and nerve myelin.
glossary.Folate: Vitamin B9, needed for DNA synthesis in dividing cells.
glossary.Gold standard: The most accurate, definitive test for a diagnosis.
glossary.Supportive care: Treatment that replaces or protects against what is missing while the cause is treated.
glossary.Blood transfusion: Giving donated red cells intravenously to raise haemoglobin.
glossary.Platelet transfusion: Giving donated platelets intravenously to prevent or stop bleeding.
glossary.Autoimmune: When the immune system attacks the body's own tissues.
glossary.Toxin: A poisonous substance that can damage cells, such as the marrow.
glossary.DNA synthesis: Making new DNA, required every time a cell divides.
glossary.Nosebleeds: Bleeding from the nose (epistaxis), a sign of low platelets.
glossary.Fever: A raised body temperature, usually 38 degrees C or more.
glossary.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
